name: Intracalcarine cortex
summary: The intracalcarine cortex is the primary visual cortex buried in the walls of the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface, the striate cortex of Brodmann area 17 named for the stria of Gennari visible to the naked eye. The upper wall receives the contralateral lower visual field and the lower wall the upper field, with the macula represented at the occipital pole and the far periphery at the anterior end near the parieto-occipital junction. It is supplied by the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery, so a PCA occlusion produces a congruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing; bilateral destruction causes cortical blindness and, with unawareness, Anton syndrome.

anatomy.location: Cortex lining the calcarine sulcus from the occipital pole forward to its junction with the parieto-occipital sulcus, between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below, facing the falx and the contralateral calcarine cortex.

efferents.to: Cuneus, lingual gyrus and lateral occipital cortex (V2-V5)

function: Striate cortex receives the geniculocalcarine radiation in layer IV, where the stria of Gennari marks the dense myelinated input, and analyzes the retinal image into oriented edges, spatial frequencies, binocular disparity and color contrast within a precise retinotopic map in which the central few degrees occupy the posterior half. It sends its output to the surrounding extrastriate areas on the cuneus and lingual gyrus and to the dorsal and ventral streams, and it projects back to the lateral geniculate nucleus and to the superior colliculus. Destructive lesions cause a congruous field defect in the contralateral hemifield, and irritative lesions cause elementary hallucinations of flashes and colored shapes in the corresponding location.

bestView.label: calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface
striate cortex within the calcarine fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The deep horizontal calcarine sulcus on medial sagittal images, running from the occipital pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus; on high-resolution T1 images the stria of Gennari appears as a thin dark line within the gray matter.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the calcarine cortex and adjacent cuneus and lingual gyrus; the occipital pole is often spared through MCA collaterals.
Bilateral calcarine infarcts, typically from basilar or bilateral PCA occlusion, with blindness that the patient denies.
Elementary visual hallucinations in the contralateral field followed by ictal blindness or eye deviation; occipital spikes accentuated by eye closure.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Destruction of the whole calcarine cortex of one side
Lesion confined to the upper (lower field) or lower (upper field) calcarine bank
Bilateral striate destruction; the pupillary pathway leaves the visual pathway before the cortex

examination: Confrontation fields in all quadrants and formal perimetry
Pupillary light reflexes, which are normal in cortical visual loss
Ask about awareness of the deficit and check for confabulation about what is seen
pearls: A hemianopia with normal pupils and macular sparing is calcarine cortex, not optic tract
Cortical blindness with denial is Anton syndrome; the patient walks into furniture and blames the light
The macula sits at the occipital pole where MCA and PCA branches overlap, which is why it survives a PCA occlusion

pitfalls: Cortical visual loss with a normal fundus and normal pupils is often called functional; perimetry and MRI settle it
